findings.claim: The previous ref cleanup is invoked but its entry is never removed from `refCleanupMap`, so a stale cleanup can be invoked a second time when the new ref produces no cleanup.
findings.rationale: `refCleanupMap.get(container)?.()` only reads the map. If the code below this hunk stores the new cleanup conditionally (e.g. `cleanup && refCleanupMap.set(...)`), then for a null/object-style ref the old closure remains registered and will run again on the next applyProps or at unmount, double-detaching. Adding `refCleanupMap.delete(container)` (or setting unconditionally) would close this. Medium confidence - depends on the not-shown lines that write to the map.

findings.claim: The old cleanup now runs on every applyProps for the `ref` key, even when the ref value is identical to the previous render, causing a spurious detach/re-attach.
findings.rationale: Unless applyProps short-circuits on unchanged attribute values, a stable function ref will now observe ref(null) followed by ref(el) on each re-render, which is a visible behavior change for callers doing imperative setup/teardown. Moderate confidence - hinges on whether the enclosing loop skips unchanged props.

findings.claim: A throwing user-supplied cleanup will propagate out of applyProps, aborting the remaining prop application and leaving the ref map inconsistent.
findings.rationale: The cleanup is user code invoked with no try/catch; previously it was only invoked at teardown time. Now an exception escapes mid-update, leaving the element partially rendered and the stale entry still in the map. Lower severity but a genuine error-handling gap.
